strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant inefficiency in synthetic multimodal learning: decoding generated 3D/audio representations into raw signals only to encode them again. Directly consuming generator latents is intuitive and potentially useful.
The proposed pipeline is clearly motivated and visually communicated. DLA, multimodal-teacher training, and MESSy distillation are easy to distinguish conceptually.

The reported accuracy gains are substantial and consistent across the three evaluated datasets. In particular, the latent teacher improves over both image-only and decoded-raw teachers, while the visual-only MESSy student improves over KD and the reported LUGPI baseline.

The experiments include modality ablations, raw-versus-latent comparisons, three-run variability, generation-time/VRAM measurements, and an attempt to analyze the student's representation rather than reporting accuracy alone.
Discarding MESSy's auxiliary heads at test time gives the visual student no additional inference cost, which is attractive for deployment.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is not established. Both auxiliary latents are generated from the input image using large pretrained models; they may therefore provide semantic transformations of the image rather than genuine audio or 3D physical information. Removing literal class names from captions does not remove synonyms, attributes, or other label-revealing cues. Poor accuracy from an auxiliary modality alone does not rule out shortcutting or complementary label leakage.

The Data Processing Inequality argument is overstated and partly misapplied. It only provides a generic information ordering under the assumed Markov chain; it does not establish that decoding injects noise, that generator latents are 'pristine,' or that any information lost is label-relevant. Controlled analyses of latent contents and decoder effects are needed.

The raw-versus-latent comparison changes the downstream representation and encoders: raw point clouds use a PointNet++-style tokenizer and audio uses a spectrogram patch embedder, whereas latents use Perceiver processing. Without matching parameter counts, token budgets, optimization, and encoder quality, the large gains cannot be attributed specifically to bypassing decoding.

MESSy's technical novelty appears limited. Predicting teacher features through learned projection heads at multiple layers is closely related to established feature-distillation methods, yet the related-work discussion is unusually sparse and does not position the method adequately against modern projector/adaptor-based distillation. The claim that direct matching necessarily causes 'geometric isomorphism' or distorts decision boundaries is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The key distillation comparison is under-specified. It is unclear whether LUGPI is reimplemented simply as L2 feature matching under exactly the same latent teacher, layers, loss weights, and parameter budget. There are no comparisons with stronger feature/logit distillation methods, normalized or relational losses, single-layer predictive heads, or parameter-matched MLP adapters.

The teacher and student are both described as ViT-B/16, conflicting with repeated claims that the student is lightweight or lower-capacity. Training recipes, initialization/pretraining, augmentations, loss weights, schedules, prompt templates, generation sampling, and dataset splits are largely absent, preventing reproducibility.

Evaluation is narrow: Imagenette, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100 are small or subset benchmarks, with no full-scale ImageNet, fine-grained recognition, distribution shift, robustness, or genuinely multimodal dataset. The unusually low image-only results also make the training setup and practical competitiveness difficult to assess.

The 'emergent synesthesia' evidence is not rigorous enough to support the strong representation claims. The clustering algorithm, ground-truth modality construction, sample protocol, and uncertainty are unspecified; label/category structure can confound NMI; and the claimed low overlap analysis is deferred to unavailable supplementary material. The class examples likewise appear selected post hoc.

Important evidence is repeatedly deferred to supplementary material—generation details, runtime measurements, the K ablation, and cluster-overlap analysis—but the supplied manuscript contains no supplement. There is also no code or sufficiently complete implementation description.

The paper provides no explicit limitations, data/model licensing discussion, or analysis of the substantial offline cost and dependencies of Gemma3, Hunyuan3D-2, and Audiocraft. These omissions matter for the claimed efficiency and reproducibility. Overall, the idea and preliminary results have merit, but confounding comparisons, possible semantic leakage, limited baselines, and insufficient methodological detail prevent a convincing Algorithms/General contribution at present.

strengths: The central idea—using undecoded generative latents as privileged training information—is intuitively appealing and relevant to efficient multimodal learning. The reported offline savings are potentially useful: bypassing decoding reduces 3D generation time by 87.7% and audio generation time by 20.6%.

The empirical gains are large and consistent across Imagenette2, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100. The latent teacher substantially outperforms both image-only and decoded-raw teachers, while the visual-only MESSy student improves over the reported KD and LUGPI baselines.

The paper includes useful modality ablations, three-run results, a comparison with decoded synthetic signals, and representation-alignment analysis. The overall three-phase pipeline is communicated clearly in Figure 2.

No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that category, the combination of direct latent augmentation and multimodal-to-unimodal transfer has some practical novelty and computer-vision relevance.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is not sufficient to establish the paper's central interpretation. The audio and 3D signals are generated from each input image rather than independently observed physical modalities. Audio additionally passes through an image-captioning model. Consequently, the gains may reflect semantic features inherited from large pretrained generators—not acoustic or geometric 'physical priors' or properties the model has 'never directly observed.'

The claimed leakage test is unconvincing. Audio-only reaches 54.61% and 3D-only 68.53% on the 10-class Imagenette benchmark, far above the 10% chance rate. Being weaker than the image model does not demonstrate absence of target-semantic leakage. Removing literal class names from captions also does not prevent synonyms, descriptions, or generator representations from encoding the class. Caption audits, label-prediction controls, shuffled-pair controls, and class-conditional leakage analyses are needed.

The raw-versus-latent comparison is confounded by substantially different representations and encoders: raw point clouds use a PointNet++-style tokenizer and spectrograms use a convolutional embedding, whereas generator latents use Perceiver blocks. Parameter counts, training budgets, token counts, encoder quality, and initialization are not controlled. Thus Table 1 does not isolate harm from decoding, and it cannot support the assertion that decoding noise causes the accuracy gap.

The Data Processing Inequality argument does not justify the paper's conclusion. It only states non-increase of mutual information along the assumed Markov chain; it neither proves a strict information loss at decoding nor shows that latent information is usable or task-relevant. The stated deterministic chain also sits awkwardly with the claim that decoding 'injects' noise.

MESSy appears technically close to standard multi-layer feature regression with learned projection/prediction heads and an MSE loss. Indeed, Equation 1 still minimizes an L2 feature-prediction error. The manuscript does not adequately distinguish this formulation from FitNets, projector-based distillation, cross-modal feature prediction, or other modern representation-distillation methods. Comparing only KD and one LUGPI implementation is too narrow to substantiate originality or the claimed resolution of 'capacity interference.'

Key comparisons and implementation details are absent. The paper does not report optimization settings, initialization or pretraining, data splits, augmentation, prompt templates, filtering rules, generator sampling settings, head architectures, loss weights, parameter/FLOP counts, or full runtime conditions. Multiple essential results are deferred to an unavailable supplementary material. This makes the unusually low image-only ViT-B results—55.10% on Caltech101 and 61.57% on ImageNet-100—particularly concerning and prevents reproducibility assessment.

Teacher and student are both described as ViT-B/16, despite the student being called 'lightweight.' There is no evaluation with genuinely smaller students, heterogeneous architectures, established full-scale benchmarks, distribution shifts, or real multimodal data. Evaluation is limited to three small classification subsets, so scalability and generality remain unclear.

The NMI experiment does not convincingly establish 'emergent synesthesia.' The supposedly ground-truth modality structures appear to derive from synthetic/generated modalities; clustering procedures and sample sizes are underspecified; class semantics can simultaneously drive visual, CLAP, and PointNet clusters; and no label-controlled, shuffled, or adjusted-NMI analysis is provided. The qualitative selection of a few favorable classes is also vulnerable to post-hoc interpretation.

Efficiency reporting covers selected offline decoder stages rather than the complete pipeline, which includes Gemma captioning, Hunyuan3D diffusion, AudioCraft, latent storage, teacher training, and distillation. End-to-end compute, storage, hardware, and environmental costs are missing, weakening the practical-efficiency claim.

The related-work discussion and attribution are too sparse for the breadth of the claims, and the paper provides no meaningful limitations, licensing/data-governance, or societal-impact discussion. Several strong statements—such as 'pristine' latents, 'true complementary physical priors,' and confirmed capacity interference—go materially beyond what the evidence establishes. Overall, the idea has merit, but confounded experiments, weak controls, limited baselines, and inadequate reproducibility evidence favor rejection.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution. The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/76d503819b114169ab563148d80fd35e/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} presents a simple and appealing idea: consume generative-model latents directly as privileged information, avoiding the costly decode-then-re-encode pipeline.

The empirical gains are consistent and practically meaningful. The latent teacher outperforms the decoded-raw teacher on all three datasets, by 4.82, 7.39, and 6.19 percentage points on Imagenette2, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100, respectively.

The visual-only MESSy student consistently improves over the image baseline, standard KD, and the stated LUGPI baseline. Its margins over LUGPI are appreciable, including 3.40 points on Caltech101 and 2.84 points on ImageNet-100.

The modality-combination study is useful: audio and 3D each improve the image teacher, while their combination performs best across all benchmarks. Reporting means and deviations over three independent runs also strengthens the evidence.
The method preserves unimodal inference and discards its auxiliary prediction heads at deployment, making the contribution relevant to practical vision systems with unavailable auxiliary modalities.

The paper is concise, clearly motivated, and supported by an effective overview figure. The offline generation-time and memory reductions indicate that direct latent use can offer benefits beyond classification accuracy.
weaknesses: The central causal explanations are stronger than the evidence supports. The data-processing inequality only states that deterministic processing cannot increase mutual information; it does not establish that decoding necessarily injects harmful noise or that undecoded latents are semantically purer. Similarly, the reported results do not directly demonstrate that L2 matching distorts the student's visual manifold through "capacity interference."

The comparison in Table 3 appears to entangle two changes: access to the proposed latent teacher and use of the MESSy objective. A decisive ablation should distill the same latent teacher using direct L2 matching, normalized or projected feature matching, and other modern feature-distillation objectives with matched layers and loss weights. Comparing mainly with KD and LUGPI is insufficient to isolate MESSy's contribution.

The raw-versus-latent comparison is not fully controlled because raw point clouds and spectrograms use PointNet++-style and convolutional tokenizers, whereas latents use Perceiver blocks. Differences in encoder capacity, token budget, optimization, and preprocessing could partly explain the accuracy gap. End-to-end storage and teacher-training costs are also absent from the efficiency analysis.

The claim that isolated modalities rule out generative shortcuts is not convincing. Audio-only accuracy reaches 54.61% on the ten-class Imagenette benchmark, far above chance, despite class-name filtering. Because audio is generated from an image-derived caption and 3D is also generated from the input image, both may encode semantic label proxies rather than complementary physical observations. Filtering literal class names does not eliminate this possibility.

The "emergent synesthesia" evidence needs a more rigorous protocol. Clustering details, variance or significance, controls for class-label mediation, and a clear definition of the allegedly ground-truth multimodal clusters are missing. Since MESSy explicitly trains the student to predict these modality features, increased NMI is expected and alone does not establish an emergent physical topology.

Evaluation is limited to three relatively small or reduced image-classification datasets and does not include a full-scale benchmark, fine-grained task, distribution shift, downstream transfer, or genuine paired multimodal data. This limits confidence that the method generalizes beyond the selected closed-set setting.

Reproducibility details are deferred to an unavailable supplement, including generation settings and the ablation over the number of distilled layers. Important main-paper details such as loss weights, training schedules, initialization, data splits, clustering algorithms, and whether synthetic data are generated exclusively from training images are underspecified. Equation 1 also appears to sum from L-K through L inclusively, yielding K+1 layers despite the text stating K layers.

The related-work coverage is narrow for an ECCV submission, particularly around multimodal knowledge distillation, latent-feature supervision, projector-based feature distillation, and synthetic multimodal augmentation. Broader and stronger baselines would better establish originality relative to these areas.

strengths: The paper presents a useful and intuitive Algorithms/General contribution: directly consuming intermediate 3D and audio generator latents avoids unnecessary decoding and re-encoding, while MESSy predicts modality-specific teacher features through auxiliary heads.

The empirical gains are substantial and consistent across Imagenette2, Caltech101, ImageNet-100, and a full ImageNet-1K experiment. Reporting three-run means and standard deviations for most core experiments is appreciated.

The evaluation includes several informative components: raw-versus-latent teachers, modality-combination studies, comparisons with logit KD and direct feature matching, target/objective ablations, and measurements of generation time and memory.
The method preserves image-only inference and discards its auxiliary prediction heads after training, making the deployment setting practically relevant.
The manuscript is generally clear, well organized, and visually effective, and it relates MESSy to predictive representation learning rather than presenting the head design without context.
weaknesses: The information-theoretic justification is overstated. Data processing only gives a non-strict inequality for the deterministic chain Z to decoded data to encoded features; it neither proves that decoding injects label-destroying noise nor guarantees that a practical classifier using Z has a higher achievable accuracy. Likewise, adding modalities cannot reduce mutual information in an unconstrained joint variable, but this does not guarantee useful complementary information under finite model capacity. Claims of a theoretical guarantee and empirical validation 'in line with DPI' should therefore be substantially weakened.

The central raw-versus-latent comparison does not isolate representation quality. Raw point clouds and spectrograms require materially different tokenizers and inductive biases; routing them through a Perceiver does not equalize encoder quality, token budgets, parameter counts, optimization difficulty, or access to strong pretrained encoders. Consequently, Table 1 can show that the chosen latent pipeline is better than the chosen raw pipeline, but not that decoding inherently degrades semantic information. Comparisons using competitive pretrained raw-modality encoders and matched compute/capacity are needed.

All purported auxiliary modalities are generated from the same input image, with audio additionally passing through a powerful vision-language model. Thus, the method transfers priors from large pretrained generators rather than obtaining physical information about the depicted instance. Stronger controls are needed against simpler ways of exploiting those priors, such as distilling Gemma/Hunyuan conditioning features, image captions, CLIP/DINO features, or an image-only teacher trained with comparable external supervision and compute.

The label-leakage analysis is insufficient. Poor audio-only or 3D-only accuracy does not rule out partial class leakage that can still benefit fusion. Filtering literal class names and WordNet synonyms misses descriptive phrases, hypernyms, dataset-correlated prompts, and knowledge memorized by the pretrained generators. This is especially important because the reported improvements are largest on object-category benchmarks potentially represented in generator pretraining.

The claims of 'genuine structural synesthesia' and physical-topology transfer are not established by the NMI analysis. MFCCs, spectral statistics, PointNet features, and geometric covariance can correlate strongly with category identity; improved classification alone may therefore increase NMI. Cluster-count choices are also ad hoc, and uncertainty, random/permutation baselines, and label-controlled alignment tests are absent.

The CIFAR-100 linear-probe result is useful but does not demonstrate the proposed capacity-interference mechanism or justify the statement that the gap can only be attributed to geometric distortion. Direct gradient-conflict measurements, visual-task retention tradeoffs, and controls matching loss weights and head capacity would be more diagnostic.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting are incomplete in the supplied manuscript. It repeatedly defers prompts, generation settings, ablations, and pipeline details to supplementary material that is not present. Total end-to-end generation/training cost, storage, hardware, batch size, learning rate, data preprocessing, splits, augmentation, and ImageNet-1K variance are not adequately reported; some Table 4 raw-teacher results are marked only with approximate values.

The student and teacher are both ViT-B/16, so descriptions of a 'lightweight' student are inaccurate. Moreover, the image-only baseline is comparatively weak, making it unclear how much of the gain survives stronger modern training recipes or pretrained image-only baselines.

MESSy's predictor-head principle is closely related to established projector-based distillation and predictive embedding methods acknowledged by the paper. The modality-specific targets are a reasonable adaptation, but the novelty is incremental and should be framed more cautiously. Overall, the promising empirical result supports a close decision, but the confounded comparisons and overclaimed causal interpretation currently favor rejection.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant inefficiency in synthetic multimodal training: decoding generated 3D/audio signals only to encode them again. Directly consuming generator latents is a sensible systems and representation-design idea.

The proposed pipeline is clearly organized into latent generation, multimodal-teacher training, and image-only distillation. The Perceiver-based handling of heterogeneous latent sequences is technically reasonable.

The reported improvements are substantial and broadly consistent across Imagenette, Caltech101, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K. The paper also reports three-run variation for most smaller-scale accuracy results and includes modality, raw-versus-latent, and prediction-target ablations.

The efficiency measurements support the narrower claim that omitting the final decoder reduces augmentation cost, particularly the reported 87.7% reduction in 3D generation time. The image-only student has no auxiliary-modality cost at inference.
weaknesses: The central information-theoretic argument is incorrect or substantially overstated. The data-processing inequality only establishes a non-increasing mutual-information bound along a Markov chain; it does not show that decoding injects harmful noise, that latent features must classify better, or that DLA has a strictly higher useful-information bound. Moreover, because both synthetic modalities are generated from the input image, they cannot add label information conditional on that image; improvements are better understood as transferring priors from large pretrained generators.

The label-leakage analysis is not convincing. Removing class names and WordNet synonyms from audio captions does not prevent indirect semantic descriptions, and Hunyuan3D is conditioned directly on the image. Audio-only accuracy of 13.07% and especially 3D-only accuracy of 39.20% on ImageNet-100 demonstrate substantial class information in the generated representations; being below the RGB baseline does not rule out shortcut learning or leakage.

The raw-versus-latent comparison does not isolate damage caused by decoding. Raw meshes and waveforms are processed by newly trained PointNet-style and spectrogram-convolution encoders, whereas generator latents already contain strong learned representations. Even Raw+Perceiver does not make the inputs or upstream representation quality equivalent. Comparisons with strong pretrained 3D/audio encoders, controlled parameter and token budgets, and frozen decoder outputs are needed before attributing the gap to decoding artifacts.

MESSy has limited methodological novelty. It is principally multilayer feature prediction through MLP projectors, closely related to FitNets, BYOL/data2vec, JEPA, and projector-based cross-modal distillation discussed by the paper itself. Evaluation against only logit KD and one direct-L2 LUGPI adaptation is too narrow; stronger feature-distillation and relational/contrastive baselines are missing.

The evidence for 'capacity interference' is insufficient. A single CIFAR-100 linear probe cannot establish the proposed mechanism, and the claim that the difference 'can only' arise from the objective ignores optimization, regularization, and projector-capacity effects. Gradient-conflict measurements, capacity sweeps, and comparisons to normalized, contrastive, or learned-projector matching would be necessary.

The 'emergent synesthesia' analysis is circular and overinterpreted. MESSy is explicitly optimized to predict auxiliary features, so increased NMI with clusters derived from those modalities is expected. Hand-crafted acoustic or geometric statistics can still correlate strongly with object class, contrary to the claim that their alignment cannot arise from class co-occurrence. There are no uncertainty estimates, sensitivity studies for cluster count, permutation controls, or evaluation on independently collected real audio/3D data.

The image-only baselines appear weak for ViT-B/16, especially 64.17% on ImageNet-1K after only 50 epochs. This makes it unclear how much of the reported gain would survive modern training recipes, pretrained visual models, longer schedules, or competitive distillation baselines. The paper also does not provide variance for ImageNet-1K.

The efficiency story accounts mainly for the omitted decoder but not the complete cost of running Gemma-3-12B, AudioGen, and Hunyuan3D over as many as 1.28 million images, storing the latents, and training a teacher over 200 extra tokens. End-to-end wall-clock, storage, energy, and compute comparisons against ordinary visual pretraining or augmentation are required for the broad efficiency claims.

Important reproducibility details and validations are deferred to unspecified supplementary material, including prompts, generation parameters, leakage filtering, efficiency protocols, and key ablations. Table 4 additionally reports approximate raw-teacher results without standard deviations. These omissions are consequential because they concern the main controls.

Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution because no type is declared. Although the idea and reported gains have merit, the confounded comparisons, weak baselines, invalid theoretical extrapolations, and unsupported causal claims prevent a convincing scientific case in the current form.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant Algorithms/General contribution: Direct Latent Augmentation bypasses decoding and re-encoding synthetic 3D and audio data, while MESSy transfers the resulting privileged information to an RGB-only student.

The central empirical results are strong and consistent. Latent teachers outperform image-only and decoded-synthetic teachers across Imagenette, Caltech101, and ImageNet-100; MESSy also improves the RGB-only student by 4.60, 8.42, and 6.97 percentage points, respectively.

The evaluation usefully separates several factors through modality ablations, a Raw+Perceiver control, comparisons with logit KD and LUGPI-style feature matching, a CLS-prediction ablation, and three-run means with standard deviations for the principal experiments.

Scaling the method to all 1.28M ImageNet-1K training images substantially strengthens the practical case: the reported RGB-only student gains 4.88 points without auxiliary modalities or heads at inference.
The efficiency motivation is compelling and quantified: bypassing decoding reportedly reduces 3D generation time by 87.7% and audio generation time by 20.6%, with meaningful peak-memory savings.

The method is clearly explained and situated relative to LUPI, generated privileged information, predictive representation learning, and feature-level distillation. The paper also acknowledges that predictive heads are related to BYOL/data2vec/JEPA rather than presenting that pattern as wholly new.

The manuscript is visually polished, and its diagrams and tables make the three-stage pipeline and main comparisons easy to understand. weaknesses: The information-theoretic argument is overstated. Data processing only gives a non-strict upper-bound ordering for a fixed Markov chain; it does not establish that the decoder necessarily injects harmful noise, that finite-capacity classifiers can exploit the latent representation more effectively, or that adding modalities supplies nonredundant information. These points are empirical hypotheses rather than theoretical guarantees.

The raw-versus-latent comparison remains imperfectly controlled. Raw data require modality-specific tokenization, whereas the proposed inputs inherit representations learned by powerful generative models. Raw+Perceiver helps, but the paper provides too little architectural and compute detail to determine whether encoder capacity, optimization, token budget, or representation itself explains the entire gap.

The MESSy comparison set is narrow. Its use of asymmetric prediction heads and multilayer targets is closely related to established projector-based distillation and predictive-learning methods, yet experiments primarily compare against KD and one LUGPI-style L2 baseline. Stronger controls such as FitNet/projector matching, CRD, normalized feature regression, and single-versus-multilayer prediction would better establish the specific novelty.

The claimed evidence of “genuine structural synesthesia” is not conclusive. MFCCs and geometric covariance can correlate with object classes, so higher NMI can arise through shared class semantics or the common source image. Label-conditioned or within-class alignment tests, permutation controls, statistical uncertainty, and evaluation against real rather than generated auxiliary observations are needed before asserting that label co-occurrence cannot explain the result.

The leakage analysis is reassuring but insufficient. Poor audio-only or 3D-only accuracy does not rule out partial shortcuts, and filtering literal class names and WordNet synonyms does not exclude paraphrases or highly diagnostic captions. Reporting filtered-caption rates, examples, a caption-only baseline, and results with class-balanced or label-obscured controls would strengthen the case.

Efficiency reporting focuses on the decoder portion rather than end-to-end dataset construction, storage, I/O, and teacher training. Because Gemma-3-12B, AudioGen, and Hunyuan3D are substantial dependencies, total GPU-hours and disk footprint are important for substantiating the practical-efficiency claim.

Reproducibility details in the supplied manuscript are incomplete: exact prompts, latent tensor shapes, raw encoders, optimizer settings, augmentations, dataset splits, generation parameters, hardware, and full loss implementation are deferred or omitted. Table 4 contains approximate raw-teacher results, and the ImageNet-1K experiment has no variance estimate.

Some language should be moderated. The teacher and student both use ViT-B/16, so “lightweight student” refers mainly to its unimodal inference path rather than a smaller backbone; selected best-improvement classes in the qualitative analysis are illustrative but not independent evidence of mechanism. These concerns limit certainty but do not outweigh the paper’s useful idea and substantial empirical gains.
